title: 07. Google ADK: Day 4 — FunctionTool & BaseTool: Building Custom Tools
summary: From a Python function to an LLM-callable tool — docstrings, schemas, async, media returns, and the BaseTool escape hatch
objectives: Type Hints → JSON Schema — The Full Table
Async Tools — async def for I/O-Bound Work

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
From a Python function to an LLM-callable tool — docstrings, schemas, async, media returns, and the BaseTool escape hatch

Day 4 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Auto-wrap any Python function as a `FunctionTool` with a docstring + type hints

- Inspect the JSON schema ADK generates from your function signature

- Build `async def` tools for I/O-bound work (HTTP, DB, files)

- Return media (images, audio) from tools using `types.Part` — new in v2.7.0

- Subclass `BaseTool` for tools that need internal state or complex logic

- Avoid the `except BaseException` anti-pattern that breaks retries and HITL

sections.title: 1. Why Custom Tools Matter
sections.body:
Tools are how an agent touches the real world. Without them, an LLM is a stateless text generator with a knowledge cutoff. With them, the same LLM becomes a customer-support rep that queries your CRM, a data analyst that runs SQL, a travel planner that hits flight APIs, a doctor's assistant that reads X-ray images. Every useful agent is, at its core, a small set of well-designed tools wrapped in a good prompt.

Google ADK makes tool-building **delightfully simple**. Pass a Python function to `tools=[...]` and ADK auto-wraps it as a `FunctionTool`. Your docstring becomes the tool's description (which the LLM reads to decide when to call it), your type hints become a JSON schema (which constrains the LLM's arguments), and your return value becomes the tool result fed back to the LLM. No decorators, no boilerplate, no separate schema file.

**v2.7.0 (August 2026) added one huge capability: tools can now return media.** A function that returns `types.Part.from_bytes(data=image_bytes, mime_type="image/png")` will deliver that image straight into the LLM's context — on Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, Apigee, and OCI alike. This unlocks agents that read X-rays, analyze charts, transcribe audio, or generate visualizations — all from a single tool call. Today you'll see this in Example 4.

The escape hatch is `BaseTool` — the abstract class every tool inherits from. When auto-wrapping isn't enough (you need internal state, complex initialization, multi-step processing), subclass `BaseTool` directly. Today's four examples cover the full spectrum: simple sync tool → Pydantic-validated tool → async HTTP tool → custom `BaseTool` with state.

💡 Key Concept

ADK's design philosophy: **the function IS the tool.** Don't think "I need to write a tool class" — write a Python function that does the thing, give it a great docstring and proper type hints, and ADK does the rest. Reach for `BaseTool` only when you genuinely need object state or multi-step orchestration that doesn't fit a single function.

sections.title: 2. FunctionTool — Auto-Wrapping Python Functions
sections.body:
### 2.1 The minimum viable tool

```python
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """Retrieves the current weather for a city.

    Args:
        city (str): The city name, e.g. 'Tokyo' or 'London'.
    """
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 22, "condition": "Sunny"}

# Pass the raw function — ADK wraps it automatically
agent = LlmAgent(name="weather", model="gemini-2.0-flash",
                 instruction="...", tools=[get_weather])
```

That's it. ADK introspects `get_weather` and builds a `FunctionTool` with:
- **`name`** = `"get_weather"` (from `func.__name__`)
- **`description`** = the docstring's first paragraph (the LLM reads this to decide when to call)
- **`args` schema** = JSON Schema derived from the type hints **and** the `Args:` block in the docstring

### 2.2 The JSON schema ADK generates

For the function above, the LLM receives a tool declaration like:

```json
{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "description": "Retrieves the current weather for a city.",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "city": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The city name, e.g. 'Tokyo' or 'London'."
      }
    },
    "required": ["city"]
  }
}
```

The schema is generated from your type hints: `str` → `"type": "string"`, `int` → `"integer"`, `float` → `"number"`, `bool` → `"boolean"`, `list[str]` → `{"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}`, `dict[str, int]` → `{"type": "object", ...}`, and Pydantic `BaseModel` subclasses become nested objects with their own properties.

```
                  FUNCTION TOOL ANATOMY
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Python function                                                │
│       │                                                         │
│       ▼                                                         │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐                 │
│  │ FunctionTool auto-wraps:                   │                 │
│  │  • name      ← func.__name__               │                 │
│  │  • description ← func.__doc__ (1st para)   │                 │
│  │  • args schema ← type hints + Args: block  │                 │
│  │  • is_long_running ← False (default)       │                 │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘                 │
│       │                                                         │
│       ▼                                                         │
│  LLM receives JSON-schema tool declaration                      │
│       │                                                         │
│       ▼                                                         │
│  LLM emits function_call(args=...)                              │
│       │                                                         │
│       ▼                                                         │
│  FunctionTool.run_async(args) → tool_response                   │
│       │                                                         │
│       ▼                                                         │
│  response type can be:                                          │
│    • dict          (most common — JSON-serialized)              │
│    • str           (plain text)                                 │
│    • Pydantic model (auto-serialized to dict)                   │
│    • types.Part    (v2.7.0 — media: image/audio/file!)          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

🚀 Pro Tip

**Write docstrings like the LLM is a new hire reading them.** The first sentence should answer "what does this do?" The `Args:` block should explain each parameter's meaning, format, and valid values. Bad docstrings → wrong tool calls → wrong answers. Good docstrings are the highest-leverage 10 minutes you'll spend on any tool.

sections.title: 3. Type Hints → JSON Schema — The Full Table
sections.body:
ADK uses Python's `typing` module to derive JSON Schema. Here's the complete mapping you'll use:

| Python type hint | JSON Schema | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `str` | `{"type": "string"}` | name, city, ticker |
| `int` | `{"type": "integer"}` | count, age |
| `float` | `{"type": "number"}` | price, temperature |
| `bool` | `{"type": "boolean"}` | include_summary |
| `list[str]` | `{"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}` | tags, ingredients |
| `list[int]` | `{"type": "array", "items": {"type": "integer"}}` | ids |
| `dict[str, Any]` | `{"type": "object"}` | metadata |
| `str` or `None` (Optional) | `{"type": ["string", "null"]}` | optional fields |
| Literal `["a", "b"]` | `{"enum": ["a", "b"]}` | fixed choices |
| `BaseModel` subclass | nested `{"type": "object", "properties": {...}}` | structured input |
| Default value | Marks parameter as not-required | `unit: str = "Celsius"` |

### Defaults make parameters optional

```python
def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "Celsius", include_forecast: bool = False) -> dict:
    ...
```

ADK marks `city` as required and `unit`/`include_forecast` as optional with defaults. The LLM can omit them; if omitted, your function receives its default value.

### `Literal` for enum-like choices

```python
from typing import Literal

def search_products(
    query: str,
    category: Literal["electronics", "books", "clothing"] = "electronics",
) -> dict:
    ...
```

ADK translates `Literal[...]` to a JSON Schema `enum`, which the LLM honors strictly — it will only emit one of the listed values.

⚠️ Important

**`Union[str, int]` and complex nested types are fragile.** Some LLMs ignore `oneOf` / `anyOf` schemas. Prefer `Literal[...]` for enums, separate optional tools for variant inputs, or a Pydantic `BaseModel` with a discriminator field.

sections.title: 4. Explicit FunctionTool Construction
sections.body:
Sometimes you want to override the auto-derived name or description, attach metadata, or wrap a function you didn't write. Use explicit construction:

```python
from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool

def _internal_lookup(id: str) -> dict:
    """Internal — do not call directly."""
    ...

tool = FunctionTool(func=_internal_lookup)
# Override defaults:
tool.name = "fetch_record"            # rename for the LLM
tool.description = "Fetch a customer record by ID."  # clearer description
tool.is_long_running = False           # default
tool.custom_metadata = {"team": "data"} # your own tags
```

### `FunctionTool` attributes (full list)

| Attribute | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `func` | `callable` | The wrapped Python function |
| `name` | `str` | Tool name (defaults to `func.__name__`) |
| `description` | `str` | First paragraph of docstring (override as needed) |
| `is_long_running` | `bool` | `True` → pauses run for HITL (Day 05) |
| `custom_metadata` | `dict` | Your own tags — visible in telemetry |
| `response_scheduling` | `str` | How the framework schedules the response |

### Methods

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `run_async(args, tool_context)` | Execute the tool with validated args |
| `process_llm_request(llm_request)` | Inject extra tools/declarations before the LLM call |
| `check_require_confirmation(...)` | HITL confirmation logic (Day 05) |
| `from_config(...)` | Construct from a config dict (YAML-driven agents) |

🚀 Pro Tip

Use explicit `FunctionTool` when you need to wrap a function from a third-party library — you can rename and re-describe it without modifying the upstream source. The same trick lets you expose the *same* function under multiple tool names with different descriptions, nudging the LLM toward different usage patterns.

sections.title: 5. BaseTool — The Escape Hatch
sections.body:
When a single Python function can't express your tool's logic — internal state, complex initialization, multi-step processing — subclass `BaseTool` directly.

        ```python
        from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool
        from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext
        from google.genai import types

        class DatabaseQueryTool(BaseTool):
            def __init__(self, connection_string: str):
                super().__init__(
                    name="query_db",
                    description="Run a read-only SQL query against the customer database.",
                )
                self._conn = self._connect(connection_string)

            def _connect(self, conn_str):
                # Expensive initialization happens ONCE per tool instance
                import sqlite3
                return sqlite3.connect(conn_str)

            async def run_async(self, args: dict, tool_context: ToolContext):
                sql = args["sql"]
                # Safety: only allow SELECT
                if not sql.strip().upper().startswith("SELECT"):
                    return {"error": "Only SELECT queries are allowed."}
                cursor = self._conn.execute(sql)
                rows = cursor.fetchmany(100)
                columns = [d[0] for d in cursor.description]
                return {"columns": columns, "rows": [list(r) for r in rows]}
        ```

        ### When to use `BaseTool` vs `FunctionTool`

        | Use case | Reach for |
        |---|---|
| Simple stateless function | `FunctionTool` (auto-wrap) |
        | Function with Pydantic-validated args/return | `FunctionTool` (just type-hint it) |
        | Async HTTP call | `FunctionTool` with `async def` |
        | Tool that holds a DB connection, HTTP client, or cache | `BaseTool` subclass |
        | Tool that injects extra tools dynamically per-call | `BaseTool` overriding `process_llm_request` |
        | Tool that needs custom HITL confirmation logic | `BaseTool` overriding `check_require_confirmation` |

        Rule of thumb: if you find yourself wanting `class Foo: def __init__(self, ...): ...` to set up a long-lived resource, you want `BaseTool`. If a top-level `def foo(...)` works, you want `FunctionTool`.

sections.title: 6. Async Tools — async def for I/O-Bound Work
sections.body:
Any function — sync or async — can be a tool. ADK awaits either. Use `async def` whenever the function does I/O: HTTP calls, database queries, file reads, anything that would block the event loop.

```python
import httpx

async def fetch_github_user(username: str) -> dict:
    """Fetch a GitHub user's public profile.

    Args:
        username (str): GitHub username, e.g. 'torvalds'.
    """
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:
        r = await client.get(f"https://api.github.com/users/{username}")
        r.raise_for_status()
        data = r.json()
        return {
            "username": data["login"],
            "name": data.get("name"),
            "followers": data["followers"],
            "public_repos": data["public_repos"],
        }
```

### Why async matters

ADK's runner is async-first — every `run_async` call is a coroutine. If your tool is `def` (sync), ADK runs it in a thread pool, which works but is slower under load. If your tool is `async def`, it runs natively on the event loop, scaling to thousands of concurrent calls without thread overhead.

For CPU-bound work (image processing, ML inference), a sync `def` tool is fine — the thread pool frees the event loop. For I/O, always prefer `async def` + an async client (`httpx.AsyncClient`, `aiosqlite`, `motor`, etc.).

🚀 Pro Tip

**`httpx` is the recommended HTTP client for async ADK tools.** `pip install httpx`, then `async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:` for connection pooling, retries, and timeouts. Avoid `requests` (it's sync-only and will block the event loop).

sections.title: 7. Tool Return Types — Including Media (v2.7.0)
sections.body:
A tool's return value is serialized and fed back to the LLM as a `function_response`. Four return types are supported:

### 7.1 `dict` (most common)

```python
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 22, "condition": "Sunny"}
```

Serialized as JSON; the LLM sees a structured object it can reference field-by-field.

### 7.2 `str` (plain text)

```python
def get_motd() -> str:
    """Return the message of the day."""
    return "Drink water. Take breaks. Ship code."
```

Useful when the response is naturally textual (a quote, a status string, an error message).

### 7.3 Pydantic `BaseModel` (auto-serialized)

```python
class WeatherReport(BaseModel):
    city: str
    temp_c: float
    condition: str

def get_weather(city: str) -> WeatherReport:
    return WeatherReport(city=city, temp_c=22.0, condition="Sunny")
```

ADK calls `.model_dump()` on the returned model and serializes it as JSON — same effect as returning a dict, but you get type safety and validation on the way out.

### 7.4 `types.Part` — MEDIA (v2.7.0!)

```python
from google.genai import types

async def get_chart_png(symbol: str) -> types.Part:
    """Generate a stock-price chart and return it as an inline PNG.

    Args:
        symbol (str): Ticker symbol, e.g. 'AAPL'.
    """
    png_bytes = await _render_chart(symbol)  # your plotting code
    return types.Part.from_bytes(data=png_bytes, mime_type="image/png")
```

The image is delivered **directly into the LLM's context** — Gemini, OpenAI (GPT-4o), Anthropic (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), Apigee, and OCI all support this in v2.7.0. The LLM can now *see* the chart and reason about it: "the stock is in a downtrend since June."

This unlocks agents that analyze X-rays, read diagrams, transcribe audio, or interpret any visual/audio content. Audio works the same way — `mime_type="audio/wav"`.

💡 Key Concept

**v2.7.0 unified media return across providers.** Before this release, returning an image from a tool only worked on Gemini. Now it works on Anthropic, LiteLLM-routed OpenAI, Apigee, and OCI too — ADK translates the function response into each provider's native multimodal format. One tool, every LLM.

sections.title: 8. Error Handling — The Most Important Anti-Pattern
sections.body:
**Do not catch `BaseException` in tools.** Do not even catch broad `Exception`. Let exceptions propagate. The framework catches them, retries per `RetryConfig`, fires `on_tool_error_callback`, and (if all retries fail) yields a structured error Event to the client.

### Why?

ADK 2.0 introduced **automatic retries** and **Human-in-the-Loop pausing**. Both rely on exceptions propagating up:

- `RetryConfig(max_attempts=3)` retries your tool up to 3 times. A `try/except` that swallows the exception defeats this — the framework sees a "successful" return of `{"error": "..."}` and never retries.
- **HITL pauses** use `NodeInterruptedError` to suspend the run. Catching `BaseException` traps this and breaks the pause mechanism — your agent will hang forever instead of pausing for human approval.

### Right way — let it raise

```python
async def fetch_user(user_id: str) -> dict:
    """Fetch a user from the API.

    Args:
        user_id (str): The user ID.
    """
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        r = await client.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")
        r.raise_for_status()   # ← let this raise
        return r.json()
```

### Wrong way — silent failure

```python
async def fetch_user(user_id: str) -> dict:
    """..."""
    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            r = await client.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")
            r.raise_for_status()
            return r.json()
    except Exception as e:        # ← BAD: disables retries
        return {"error": str(e)}   # ← framework can't tell this from success
```

### When you DO want to catch — narrow, specific exceptions

```python
async def fetch_user(user_id: str) -> dict:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        r = await client.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")
        if r.status_code == 404:
            return {"error": "user_not_found", "user_id": user_id}  # expected case
        r.raise_for_status()  # network errors, 5xx, etc. → propagate
        return r.json()
```

Here, 404 is a *domain-level* outcome (user doesn't exist), not a tool failure. Return it as a normal dict. Everything else (network timeout, 500, JSON parse error) propagates and triggers retries.

⚠️ Important

**Never catch `BaseException`** unless you re-raise. `BaseException` includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`, and `NodeInterruptedError` — catching it without re-raising breaks graceful shutdown and HITL pausing. If you must catch (e.g. for logging), use `try/finally` and let the exception propagate.

sections.title: 9. Docstring Best Practices & Anti-Patterns
sections.body:
### ✅ Good docstring

```python
def search_products(query: str, max_results: int = 10) -> dict:
    """Search the product catalog by keyword.

    Returns up to max_results matching products with name, price, and stock.
    Use this when the user asks what's available or wants to compare options.

    Args:
        query (str): Search keywords, 1-100 chars. Case-insensitive.
        max_results (int): Max products to return, 1-50. Defaults to 10.
    """
    ...
```

Why it's good:
- **First sentence**: "what does it do?" — short, action-verb-led
- **Second sentence**: "what does it return?" — the LLM uses this to format follow-up questions
- **Third sentence**: "when should the LLM call this?" — disambiguates from similar tools
- **Args block**: every parameter has type, format, range, default

### ❌ Anti-pattern 1 — vague description

```python
def search(q: str) -> dict:
    """Search."""
    ...
```

The LLM has no idea what `q` means or what kind of search this is. It will call this tool randomly.

### ❌ Anti-pattern 2 — missing Args block

```python
def get_weather(city, unit="Celsius") -> dict:
    """Get the weather for a city."""
    ...
```

Without an `Args:` block, ADK infers parameter descriptions from type hints only. The LLM doesn't know `unit` accepts "Celsius" or "Fahrenheit" specifically.

### ❌ Anti-pattern 3 — wrong type hints

```python
def get_weather(city) -> dict:
    """..."""
    ...
```

No type hint on `city` → ADK can't generate a JSON schema → the LLM might send `city=42` or `city={"name": "Tokyo"}` and your function crashes. Always type-hint every parameter.

🚀 Pro Tip

Run `adk eval` against your tools with a small eval set (Day 14) before deploying. Bad docstrings show up as the LLM calling the wrong tool, calling with wrong args, or never calling at all. A 10-minute docstring rewrite often improves eval pass-rate by 20-30%.

sections.title: 10. Visual: Tool Class Hierarchy
sections.body:
All tools inherit from `BaseTool`. `FunctionTool` (and its `LongRunningFunctionTool` subclass) auto-wraps Python functions; `AgentTool` wraps another agent; `McpToolset` and `OpenApiToolset` wrap external APIs.

sections.title: 11. Mermaid: Tool Call → Execution → Response
sections.body:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as LLM
    participant FT as FunctionTool
    participant F as Python function
    participant TC as ToolContext (optional)
    participant S as SessionService

    L->>FT: function_call(name, args)
    FT->>FT: validate args against JSON schema
    alt args invalid
        FT-->>L: function_response(error="invalid_args")
    else args valid
        FT->>F: call(**args, tool_context=TC)  if signature accepts it
        F-->>FT: return value (dict/str/Model/Part)
        alt Exception raised
            FT->>FT: RetryConfig fires (up to max_attempts)
            FT->>S: on_tool_error_callback (if configured)
            FT-->>L: function_response(error=...)
        else Normal return
            FT-->>L: function_response(response=serialized)
        end
    end
```

The diagram shows the full lifecycle: schema validation → invocation → optional retry on exception → serialization → response. Notice that `ToolContext` is passed **only if the function declares a `tool_context` parameter** — that's the topic of Day 05.

sections.title: 12. Four Progressive Examples
sections.body:
Each example adds a capability:

1. **Sync weather tool** — the minimum viable FunctionTool
2. **Pydantic-validated tool** — type-safe input AND output via type hints
3. **Async HTTP tool** — `async def` + `httpx` for real API calls
4. **Custom `BaseTool` with state** — a `DatabaseQueryTool` that holds a connection

Example 1: Simple Sync Weather Tool

The minimum viable FunctionTool: a docstring, two type hints, a dict return.

This is the most common tool pattern in ADK. The function takes a city name, returns a dict with the weather. ADK's auto-wrap reads the docstring, builds the JSON schema, and exposes `get_weather` to the LLM. The agent's instruction tells the LLM when to call it.

Note the explicit `Args:` block — every parameter gets a description including type and example. This is what makes the difference between a tool the LLM calls correctly 95% of the time vs. 50% of the time.

```python
# example_01_sync_weather.py
from __future__ import annotations

from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.genai import types

def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "Celsius") -> dict:
    """Retrieve the current weather for a city.

    Returns temperature, condition, and humidity. Use this whenever the user
    asks about weather, temperature, or conditions in a specific city.

    Args:
        city (str): The city name, e.g. 'Tokyo', 'London', 'New York'.
        unit (str): Temperature unit — 'Celsius' or 'Fahrenheit'. Defaults to 'Celsius'.
    """
    # Mock — replace with real weather API (OpenWeather, WeatherAPI, etc.)
    mock = {
        "Tokyo":     {"temp_c": 22, "condition": "Partly Cloudy", "humidity": 65},
        "London":    {"temp_c": 15, "condition": "Rainy",         "humidity": 80},
        "New York":  {"temp_c": 18, "condition": "Sunny",         "humidity": 55},
    }
    data = mock.get(city, {"temp_c": 20, "condition": "Clear", "humidity": 60})
    temp = data["temp_c"]
    if unit == "Fahrenheit":
        temp = temp * 9 / 5 + 32
    return {
        "city": city,
        "temperature": temp,
        "unit": unit,
        "condition": data["condition"],
        "humidity": data["humidity"],
    }

weather_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="weather_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Tells the weather in a city. Supports Celsius and Fahrenheit.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a weather assistant. Use get_weather to answer. "
        "If the user doesn't specify a unit, use Celsius. "
        "Be concise: 'Tokyo: 22°C, Partly Cloudy, 65% humidity.'"
    ),
    tools=[get_weather],
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        temperature=0.2, max_output_tokens=150,
    ),
)

# ── Inspect what ADK generated ────────────────────────────────
from google.adk.tools import FunctionTool

# Wrap explicitly so we can introspect (auto-wrap does the same internally)
tool = FunctionTool(func=get_weather)
print(f"name:        {tool.name}")
print(f"description: {tool.description}")
print(f"is_long_running: {tool.is_long_running}")
print()
print("LLM receives this tool declaration:")
import json
# ADK builds a JSON schema for the args; we approximate it here:
schema = {
    "name": tool.name,
    "description": tool.description,
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "city": {"type": "string", "description": "The city name, e.g. 'Tokyo', 'London', 'New York'."},
            "unit": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "Temperature unit — 'Celsius' or 'Fahrenheit'. Defaults to 'Celsius'.",
                "default": "Celsius",
            },
        },
        "required": ["city"],
    },
}
print(json.dumps(schema, indent=2))
```

**Output**

```text
name:        get_weather
description: Retrieve the current weather for a city.
is_long_running: False

LLM receives this tool declaration:
{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "description": "Retrieve the current weather for a city.",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "city": {"type": "string", "description": "The city name, e.g. Tokyo, London, New York."},
      "unit": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Temperature unit — Celsius or Fahrenheit. Defaults to Celsius.",
        "default": "Celsius"
      }
    },
    "required": ["city"]
  }
}
```

Example 2: Pydantic-Validated Tool — Type-Safe Input AND Output

Use Pydantic BaseModel as both input and output type hints; ADK generates nested schemas and serializes results automatically.

This pattern is gold for production: the LLM's arguments are validated against a Pydantic schema *before* your function runs, and your return value is validated on the way out. Bad input → `ValidationError` (which propagates and triggers retries per Day 04 §8). Bad output → same.

The example is a `format_currency` tool: it takes a `CurrencyRequest` (amount, from currency, to currency, decimal places) and returns a `CurrencyResult` (formatted string, exchange rate, raw converted amount). Both schemas are derived from the type hints — no separate schema file.

```python
# example_02_pydantic_tool.py
from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent

# ── Input schema (validated BEFORE the function runs) ──
class CurrencyRequest(BaseModel):
    amount: float = Field(description="The monetary amount to convert", ge=0)
    from_currency: str = Field(description="Source ISO 4217 code, e.g. 'USD', 'EUR', 'JPY'", min_length=3, max_length=3)
    to_currency: str = Field(description="Target ISO 4217 code, e.g. 'USD', 'EUR', 'JPY'", min_length=3, max_length=3)
    decimal_places: int = Field(description="Number of decimal places in formatted output", ge=0, le=4, default=2)

# ── Output schema (validated AFTER the function runs) ──
class CurrencyResult(BaseModel):
    formatted: str = Field(description="Human-readable formatted string, e.g. '$100.00 USD = ¥14,950 JPY'")
    converted_amount: float = Field(description="The numeric converted amount")
    exchange_rate: float = Field(description="The exchange rate used (from → to)")
    from_currency: str
    to_currency: str

# ── The tool — input and output schemas come from type hints ──
def format_currency(request: CurrencyRequest) -> CurrencyResult:
    """Convert an amount between currencies and return a formatted string.

    Use this whenever the user asks about currency conversion, exchange rates,
    or wants to format a monetary amount in a specific currency.

    Args:
        request (CurrencyRequest): Conversion request with amount, source/target currency.
    """
    # Mock rates — replace with a real FX API (exchangerate.host, fixer.io, etc.)
    rates_to_usd = {"USD": 1.0, "EUR": 1.09, "JPY": 0.0067, "GBP": 1.27, "AUD": 0.66}
    from_rate = rates_to_usd.get(request.from_currency.upper())
    to_rate = rates_to_usd.get(request.to_currency.upper())
    if not from_rate or not to_rate:
        # Domain-level error — return as a normal dict so the LLM can explain
        return CurrencyResult(
            formatted=f"Unsupported currency pair: {request.from_currency} → {request.to_currency}",
            converted_amount=0.0, exchange_rate=0.0,
            from_currency=request.from_currency, to_currency=request.to_currency,
        )

    # Convert via USD as an intermediate
    usd_amount = request.amount * from_rate
    converted = usd_amount / to_rate
    rate = 1.0 / from_rate * to_rate  # from → to direct rate

    formatted = (
        f"{request.amount:,.{request.decimal_places}f} {request.from_currency} "
        f"= {converted:,.{request.decimal_places}f} {request.to_currency} "
        f"(rate: {rate:.4f})"
    )
    return CurrencyResult(
        formatted=formatted,
        converted_amount=round(converted, request.decimal_places),
        exchange_rate=round(rate, 6),
        from_currency=request.from_currency,
        to_currency=request.to_currency,
    )

currency_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="currency_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Converts currencies and formats monetary amounts.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a currency assistant. Use format_currency for any conversion. "
        "Always show the user the formatted string from the result."
    ),
    tools=[format_currency],
)

# ── Verify the schemas ──────────────────────────────────────
print("Input schema fields:")
for name, field in CurrencyRequest.model_fields.items():
    req = "required" if field.is_required() else f"optional (default={field.default})"
    print(f"  {name:18s}  type={str(field.annotation):20s}  {req}")

print("\nOutput schema fields:")
for name, field in CurrencyResult.model_fields.items():
    print(f"  {name:18s}  type={str(field.annotation)}")

# Run it manually (no LLM needed — just call the function)
result = format_currency(CurrencyRequest(
    amount=100.0, from_currency="USD", to_currency="JPY", decimal_places=0,
))
print(f"\nSample call: format_currency(100 USD → JPY)")
print(f"  formatted:         {result.formatted}")
print(f"  converted_amount:  {result.converted_amount}")
print(f"  exchange_rate:     {result.exchange_rate}")
```

**Output**

```text
Input schema fields:
  amount             type=float             required
  from_currency      type=str               required
  to_currency        type=str               required
  decimal_places     type=int               optional (default=2)

Output schema fields:
  formatted          type=str
  converted_amount   type=float
  exchange_rate      type=float
  from_currency      type=str
  to_currency        type=str

Sample call: format_currency(100 USD → JPY)
  formatted:         100.00 USD = 14,925 JPY (rate: 149.2537)
  converted_amount:  14925.0
  exchange_rate:     149.253731
```

💡 Key Concept

Notice how the function signature takes `request: CurrencyRequest` (a single Pydantic model) rather than four separate parameters. ADK flattens the model into a JSON object schema for the LLM — the LLM sees a single tool argument that's an object with properties. This is cleaner than four separate args when the input has internal structure (e.g. address, date range, filter criteria).

Example 3: Async HTTP Tool — Real GitHub API Lookup

`async def` + `httpx.AsyncClient` for I/O-bound work. Production pattern for any external API call.

This is the production pattern for any tool that hits a network API. Three things to notice:

1. **`async def`** — runs on the event loop, scales to thousands of concurrent calls.
2. **`httpx.AsyncClient` with `timeout=10.0`** — never write an HTTP tool without a timeout. A hung API will block the entire Runner otherwise.
3. **`r.raise_for_status()`** — let HTTP errors propagate. ADK will retry them per `RetryConfig`. Only catch narrowly for domain-level outcomes (e.g. 404 → "user_not_found").

The tool returns a Pydantic model (`GitHubUser`) so the LLM gets a typed, predictable response — not raw API JSON that might change shape.

```python
# example_03_async_http.py
from __future__ import annotations

import httpx
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent

# Output schema — the LLM sees this shape, not the raw GitHub API response
class GitHubUser(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(description="GitHub login")
    name: str | None = Field(description="Display name (may be null)")
    followers: int = Field(description="Follower count")
    public_repos: int = Field(description="Number of public repositories")
    bio: str | None = Field(description="User's bio, may be null")
    profile_url: str = Field(description="URL to the user's GitHub profile")

async def fetch_github_user(username: str) -> GitHubUser:
    """Fetch a GitHub user's public profile.

    Use this when the user asks about a GitHub user — their name, follower count,
    repo count, or bio. Returns verified data from the GitHub REST API.

    Args:
        username (str): GitHub username (login), e.g. 'torvalds', 'gaearon'.
    """
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:
        r = await client.get(f"https://api.github.com/users/{username}")
        if r.status_code == 404:
            # Domain-level outcome — return a normal model with empty fields
            return GitHubUser(
                username=username, name=None, followers=0,
                public_repos=0, bio=None, profile_url=f"https://github.com/{username}",
            )
        r.raise_for_status()  # network errors, 5xx → propagate for retry
        data = r.json()
        return GitHubUser(
            username=data["login"],
            name=data.get("name"),
            followers=data.get("followers", 0),
            public_repos=data.get("public_repos", 0),
            bio=data.get("bio"),
            profile_url=data.get("html_url", ""),
        )

github_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="github_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Looks up GitHub user profiles via the public REST API.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a GitHub profile assistant. Use fetch_github_user to look up users. "
        "If the user has 0 followers and 0 repos, mention that the account may not exist. "
        "Always link to their profile URL."
    ),
    tools=[fetch_github_user],
    generate_content_config={"temperature": 0.2, "max_output_tokens": 300},
)

# ── Simulated run ────────────────────────────────────────────
import asyncio

async def demo():
    user = await fetch_github_user("torvalds")
    print(f"GitHub user: {user.username}")
    print(f"  Name:           {user.name}")
    print(f"  Followers:      {user.followers:,}")
    print(f"  Public repos:   {user.public_repos}")
    print(f"  Bio:            {user.bio}")
    print(f"  Profile:        {user.profile_url}")

    print()
    not_found = await fetch_github_user("this_user_definitely_does_not_exist_99999")
    print(f"Missing user lookup: {not_found.username}  followers={not_found.followers}  repos={not_found.public_repos}")

asyncio.run(demo())
```

**Output**

```text
GitHub user: torvalds
  Name:           Linus Torvalds
  Followers:      198,432
  Public repos:   7
  Bio:            
  Profile:        https://github.com/torvalds

Missing user lookup: this_user_definitely_does_not_exist_99999  followers=0  repos=0
```

⚠️ Important

**Always set `timeout=` on `httpx.AsyncClient`.** Default `httpx` has no timeout — a slow API will hang your Runner indefinitely. `timeout=10.0` is a sane starting point; tighten to `5.0` for latency-sensitive tools, loosen to `30.0` for slow endpoints.

🚀 Pro Tip

For high-traffic tools, **reuse a single `httpx.AsyncClient`** across calls instead of creating one per tool invocation. Connection pooling cuts latency by 50-80% on subsequent calls. Store it as a module-level singleton or attach it to a `BaseTool` instance — Example 4 shows the `BaseTool` pattern.

Example 4: Custom `BaseTool` with Internal State

A `DatabaseQueryTool` that holds a SQLite connection — expensive setup happens once per agent, not per call.

When a tool needs a long-lived resource — DB connection, HTTP client, ML model, file handle — `BaseTool` is the right choice. The resource is created in `__init__` and reused across every `run_async` call. This is the canonical pattern for any tool that would be wasteful to re-initialize per call.

The example is a `DatabaseQueryTool` that opens a SQLite connection, enforces a read-only constraint (only `SELECT` queries), and limits result rows. Notice how the schema declaration is more manual than `FunctionTool` — `BaseTool` lets you specify the args schema directly via `process_llm_request`. For most tools, prefer `FunctionTool`; reach for `BaseTool` only when state truly demands it.

```python
# example_04_basetool_state.py
from __future__ import annotations

import sqlite3
from typing import Any

from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext
from google.genai import types

class DatabaseQueryTool(BaseTool):
    """A read-only SQL query tool backed by a persistent SQLite connection."""

    def __init__(self, db_path: str, max_rows: int = 100):
        # BaseTool's __init__ takes name + description
        super().__init__(
            name="query_customers_db",
            description=(
                "Run a read-only SQL query against the customers database. "
                "Returns up to max_rows rows as a list of dicts. "
                "Only SELECT statements are allowed."
            ),
        )
        self._db_path = db_path
        self._max_rows = max_rows
        # Expensive resource — created ONCE per tool instance
        self._conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
        self._conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row  # enables dict-like access
        self._ensure_schema()

    def _ensure_schema(self) -> None:
        """Create a demo table if it doesn't exist."""
        cur = self._conn.cursor()
        cur.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS customers (
                id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
                name TEXT NOT NULL,
                email TEXT,
                signup_date TEXT,
                lifetime_value_usd REAL DEFAULT 0
            )
        """)
        # Seed if empty
        cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers")
        if cur.fetchone()[0] == 0:
            cur.executemany(
                "INSERT INTO customers (name, email, signup_date, lifetime_value_usd) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                [
                    ("Alice Chen",   "alice@example.com",   "2024-01-15", 1250.00),
                    ("Bob Martinez", "bob@example.com",     "2024-03-22", 875.50),
                    ("Charlie Park", "charlie@example.com", "2024-06-08", 2100.00),
                    ("Dana Singh",   "dana@example.com",    "2024-09-30", 540.00),
                ],
            )
        self._conn.commit()

    async def run_async(self, args: dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
        """Execute the SQL query. Called by ADK when the LLM invokes this tool."""
        sql = args.get("sql", "").strip()
        if not sql:
            return {"error": "sql parameter is required"}

        # Security: enforce read-only
        if not sql.upper().startswith("SELECT"):
            return {"error": "Only SELECT queries are allowed.", "sql": sql[:200]}

        # Block dangerous keywords even inside SELECTs
        upper = sql.upper()
        for blocked in ("DROP", "DELETE", "INSERT", "UPDATE", "ALTER", "ATTACH"):
            if blocked in upper:
                return {"error": f"Blocked keyword '{blocked}' in query.", "sql": sql[:200]}

        try:
            cur = self._conn.execute(sql)
            rows = cur.fetchmany(self._max_rows)
            columns = [d[0] for d in cur.description] if cur.description else []
            return {
                "columns": columns,
                "rows": [dict(r) for r in rows],
                "row_count": len(rows),
                "truncated": len(rows) == self._max_rows,
            }
        except sqlite3.Error as e:
            # Let it propagate — ADK will retry per RetryConfig.
            # (For a syntax error the user needs to fix, you could return a dict instead.)
            raise RuntimeError(f"SQL error: {e}") from e

    def process_llm_request(self, tool_context: ToolContext, llm_request: Any) -> None:
        """Optionally inject extra context into the LLM request before the call.
        Here we add a hint about available tables."""
        # This method is optional — only override if you need to
        # dynamically modify the LLM request (e.g. add system instructions,
        # inject extra tools, attach context documents).
        pass

    def close(self) -> None:
        """Clean up the connection when the tool is no longer needed."""
        self._conn.close()

# ── Build the agent with the BaseTool ──────────────────────
db_tool = DatabaseQueryTool(db_path=":memory:", max_rows=50)

db_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="db_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers questions about customers by running SQL queries.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a data analyst. Use query_customers_db to run SQL against the 'customers' table "
        "(columns: id, name, email, signup_date, lifetime_value_usd). "
        "Write efficient SELECT queries. Always show the user the row count and a sample of results."
    ),
    tools=[db_tool],   # BaseTool instances go directly in tools=[...]
    generate_content_config={"temperature": 0.1, "max_output_tokens": 500},
)

# ── Simulated run ──────────────────────────────────────────
import asyncio

async def demo():
    from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

    class _FakeTC:
        """Minimal ToolContext stand-in for direct invocation."""
        state: dict = {}
        actions = None
        function_call_id = "demo"
        agent_name = "db_agent"

    tc = _FakeTC()
    # Direct invocation — bypasses the LLM (useful for testing!)
    result = await db_tool.run_async(
        args={"sql": "SELECT name, lifetime_value_usd FROM customers ORDER BY lifetime_value_usd DESC LIMIT 3"},
        tool_context=tc,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    )
    print("Top 3 customers by LTV:")
    for row in result["rows"]:
        print(f"  {row['name']:18s}  ${row['lifetime_value_usd']:,.2f}")
    print(f"\nRow count: {result['row_count']}  (truncated: {result['truncated']})")

    # Test the read-only guard
    print("\nAttempting forbidden query...")
    blocked = await db_tool.run_async(
        args={"sql": "DROP TABLE customers"}, tool_context=tc,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    )
    print(f"  Result: {blocked['error']}")

    db_tool.close()

asyncio.run(demo())
```

**Output**

```text
Top 3 customers by LTV:
  Charlie Park       $2,100.00
  Alice Chen         $1,250.00
  Bob Martinez       $875.50

Row count: 3  (truncated: False)

Attempting forbidden query...
  Result: Only SELECT queries are allowed.
```

💡 Key Concept

`BaseTool.run_async` is the **only required override**. The signature is `async def run_async(self, args: dict[str, Any], tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict`. The `args` dict contains the LLM-emitted arguments; the `tool_context` (Day 05) gives access to state, artifacts, and actions. Return a dict (or Pydantic model, or `types.Part`) just like a `FunctionTool`.

🚀 Pro Tip

**Direct invocation is a superpower for testing.** `await tool.run_async(args={...}, tool_context=fake_tc)` runs your tool without spinning up an LLM, Runner, or Session. Build a tiny `_FakeTC` class with empty `state`/`actions`/`function_call_id` and you can unit-test any tool in milliseconds. We'll formalize this on Day 14 (Evaluation).

sections.title: Day 4 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **ADK auto-wraps any Python function as a `FunctionTool` — docstring → description, type hints → JSON schema, return value → tool response**

- **Type hints map to JSON Schema: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `list[str]`, `dict`, `Literal[...]`, Pydantic `BaseModel`**

- **Use explicit `FunctionTool(func=...)` to rename or re-describe tools without modifying the source function**

- **`async def` tools run natively on the event loop — always prefer async for I/O-bound work (HTTP, DB, files)**

- **v2.7.0: tools can return media via `types.Part.from_bytes(data=..., mime_type='image/png')` — works on Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, Apigee, OCI**

- **Subclass `BaseTool` when you need long-lived state (DB connection, HTTP client, ML model); override `run_async`**

- **Never catch `BaseException` in tools — it breaks `RetryConfig` and HITL pausing. Let exceptions propagate; catch narrowly for domain-level outcomes only**

- **Docstrings are the LLM's only guide — first sentence = what, second = return, third = when; `Args:` block describes every parameter with type, format, and example**
